dataset.name: Data for: Time to anoxia: Observations and predictions of oxygen drawdown following coastal flood events
description: This dataset contains data and code associated with the paper Patel et al. "Time to anoxia: Observations and predictions of oxygen drawdown following coastal flood events".

The coastal terrestrial-aquatic interface (TAI) is a highly dynamic system characterized by strong physical, chemical, and biological gradients. In particular, shifting soil redox conditions and consumption of terminal electron acceptors, due in part to dynamic hydrologic conditions, is a strong driver of carbon availability and transformations across TAIs. However, while redox dynamics are well described, our ability to quantitatively forecast rates of oxic to anoxic shifts in soils with different characteristics and inundation regimes is limited. We integrated field measurements, laboratory incubations, and model simulations to improve mechanistic understanding of oxygen consumption dynamics in coastal soils. Continuous in situ monitoring unexpectedly revealed that flooding caused temporary spikes in subsurface dissolved oxygen followed by rapid consumption in the wetlands. To further investigate these mechanisms in a controlled setting, we performed laboratory incubations using surface and subsurface soils from a TAI gradient (defined here as upland forest to transitional forest to wetland) in Western Lake Erie to measure oxygen consumption rates in TAI soils during flood events. In our experiments, wetland soils reached anoxia the fastest, in ∼ 9 h on average, whereas upland soils turned anoxic in ∼ 18 h. Subsurface upland soils did not turn anoxic even after two weeks of saturation in the lab, and their oxygen consumption patterns suggested carbon and/or nutrient limitation. These results are consistent with in-situ groundwater redox and oxygen measurements in the field, where wetland soils exhibited the highest rates of oxygen consumption along the TAI. Model simulations of oxygen consumption suggested that oxygen consumption had stronger abiotic controls in wetland soils but stronger biotic controls in upland soils, providing a useful framework for future incubation experiments. Microbial activity is a strong driver of oxygen consumption in TAI soils, although it is constrained by the availability of dissolved carbon in subsurface soils.

This dataset contains a compressed (.zip) archive of the data and R scripts used for this manuscript. The dataset includes files in .csv format, which can be accessed and processed using MS Excel or R. This archive can also be accessed on GitHub at https://github.com/COMPASS-DOE/cmps-time_to_anoxia (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.10815374).

spatialCoverage.description: The Old Woman Creek watershed is located at Lake Erie's southern shore (lat 41.376, lon −82.508, Fig. 1A), in the Great Lakes region of the north-central U.S. The watershed is a National Estuarine Research Reserve (NERR) operated jointly between the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and the Ohio Department of Natural Resources (ODNR). It is a lacustary (lake influenced) preserve in the Huron-Erie Lake Plains Ecoregion. The soils are formed in fine textured glacio-lacustrine deposits overlaying Silurian and Devonian limestone and dolomite bedrock (Ohio EPA, 2012). Glacial advance and retreat during the late Wisconsinan glacial era has caused this region to be primarily flat and uniform with a 6 m elevation difference from wetland to upland habitat. The plant community of the Old Woman Creek watershed exhibits a range of adaptations to flooding from terrestrial plants that can withstand intermittent submergence to specifically adapted plants that thrive exclusively in aquatic environments. Uplands feature mixed hardwood forests with oak, hickory, maple, cherry, ash, and other tree species. The forest understory consists of herbaceous formations, including shrubs, small trees, abundant wildflowers, white trillium, may-apple, violets, trout-lilies, and cardinal flowers. Wetland habitats include open water areas, mud flats, marshes, swamp forests, and various shoreline types with aquatic plants such as American water lotus, arrowhead, duckweed, cattails, bulrushes, and water lilies (Herdendorf et al., 2006).

measurementTechnique:
Site description
The Old Woman Creek watershed is located at Lake Erie's southern shore (lat 41.376, lon −82.508), in the Great Lakes region of the north-central U.S. The watershed is a National Estuarine Research Reserve (NERR) operated jointly between the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and the Ohio Department of Natural Resources (ODNR). It is a lacustary (lake influenced) preserve in the Huron-Erie Lake Plains Ecoregion. The soils are formed in fine textured glacio-lacustrine deposits overlaying Silurian and Devonian limestone and dolomite bedrock (Ohio EPA, 2012). Glacial advance and retreat during the late Wisconsinan glacial era has caused this region to be primarily flat and uniform with a 6 m elevation difference from wetland to upland habitat.
The plant community of the Old Woman Creek watershed exhibits a range of adaptations to flooding from terrestrial plants that can withstand intermittent submergence to specifically adapted plants that thrive exclusively in aquatic environments. Uplands feature mixed hardwood forests with oak, hickory, maple, cherry, ash, and other tree species. The forest understory consists of herbaceous formations, including shrubs, small trees, abundant wildflowers, white trillium, may-apple, violets, trout-lilies, and cardinal flowers. Wetland habitats include open water areas, mud flats, marshes, swamp forests, and various shoreline types with aquatic plants such as American water lotus, arrowhead, duckweed, cattails, bulrushes, and water lilies (Herdendorf et al., 2006).
We established a transect along the TAI for the purpose of monitoring and soil sampling. The transect consisted of three distinct zones - upland forest, which is typically dry and terrestrial, and characterized by healthy trees; transitional forest, which undergoes periodic inundation because of bidirectional floods from upland and the lake, and is characterized by dying trees; and wetland, which is characterized by herbaceous vegetation. General site and soil characteristics are presented in the manuscript.

Groundwater oxygen monitoring
We measured in-situ groundwater dissolved oxygen concentrations (DO) and oxidative-redox potential (ORP) continuously using Aqua TROLL 600 Multiparameter Sondes (In-Situ Inc.). The sondes were deployed in wells in the transitional zone (58.5 cm depth) (Table 2) and wetland zone (34 cm depth), and measurements were taken at 15-minute intervals. An upland well was not installed at this site due to the steep topography and logistical considerations. The wells were constructed with PVC tubes with a diameter of 4.2 cm with 2.5 mm slots at 1 cm intervals that extended up to 5 cm below the surface of the soil (ESP Supply). The remaining length of the well was solid sealed at the surface with bentonite. Sensors were calibrated prior to deployment and every three months during deployment following manufacturer protocols. Using the sonde data, we identified eight inundation events (four in the transition, four in the wetland) that were accompanied by changes in DO and ORP. These events occurred as a result of a natural sand barrier at the mouth of the estuary building up intermittently with drainage occurring following breaches of the sand barrier. We recorded the maximum DO and ORP values for these inundation events, and the time needed to return to baseline anoxic conditions (DO = 0 mg/L) to determine the oxygen consumption rates in the groundwater.

Laboratory incubation
We performed a laboratory incubation to understand oxygen uptake dynamics in these soils in a controlled setting. We collected spatially replicated grab samples from each of the transect positions in December 2021. Soils were sampled from the surface A horizon (0–10 cm) from all three transect locations, as well as the B horizon (10–20 cm) from the upland forest. Eight replicates were collected per transect location, which were then homogenized to produce one bulk sample per transect location. The samples were stored at 4 °C until ready for processing and incubation.
Soil microcosms were prepared by weighing 10 g field moist soil into 50 mL centrifuge tubes and inundating with deionized MilliQ water. The water was bubbled with air before the incubation to ensure it was 100 % saturated with oxygen (i.e., 8.5 mg/L DO at 21 °C). This incubation was done in triplicate (n = 3). The tubes were completely filled with water to eliminate any headspace and then sealed shut using screw-caps fitted with transparent discs treated with a chemical coating of oxygen-sensitive dyes that produce an optode sensor as part of a metabolic multi-reactor (Kaufman et al., 2023). Optode disks were calibrated before reaction in water using precise mixing of air and nitrogen gas to produce a six point calibration curve from 0 to 100 % oxygen saturation (Kaufman et al., 2023). This was done following the same imaging procedures for the incubation reaction as detailed below.
For the incubation, the soil- and water-filled tubes were placed horizontally on a roller (<30 rpm) with the disks in the tube caps oriented to face the camera. Photographs were taken at programmed intervals using a modified digital camera (EOS Rebel T6, Canon Inc, Tokyo, Japan) with an 18.0-megapixel sensor. The experiment was conducted in the dark with the tubes continuously rolling. The roller was stopped automatically and a blue LED (450–460 nm) excitation light illuminated the optode caps when the images were taken (Kaufman et al., 2023). Image processing was done using ImageJ (Larsen et al., 2011, Schindelin et al., 2015).
Photos were taken every 15 min for 24 h and most samples were removed and destructively sampled to characterize the water (considered water extract of the soil). Extracts were stored at 4 °C and analyzed for pH and water extractable organic carbon (WEOC, determined as non-purgeable organic carbon using a Shimadzu TOC-L analyzer) (Appendix A1). One experimental replicate per soil type was kept saturated and sealed for two weeks, with photographs taken daily for the remainder of the two-week incubation. All incubation reactions were initiated and imaged at the same time while on the rollers. Oxygen consumption rates were calculated as the change in oxygen concentration divided by the time taken to reach anoxia. All samples started at 8.5 mg/L DO (100 % oxygen saturation). We defined anoxia as the point at which the DO concentrations dropped to 0 mg/L. The average oxygen consumption rates were normalized to the dry mass of soil, determined by oven-drying soils at 105 °C for 24 h.

Substrate-induced respiration
Because an appreciable fraction of oxygen consumption in our study system is presumably microbially driven, we also determined relative differences in microbial glucose consumption rates (i.e., substrate induced respiration) on a small batch of samples. 1.5 g oven-dry equivalent (ODE) subsamples were weighed into 40-mL glass vials, and a glucose saturation curve was obtained by adding 0–32 mg glucose per g of soil. The CO2 evolved after one hour was measured on an EGM-4 Infra-Red Gas Analyzer (PP Systems). The glucose saturation curve was used to determine the minimum amount of glucose that caused the maximum CO2 response, and this was used to estimate microbial biomass in our samples (Bailey et al., 2007).

Modeling DO depletion during incubations
For insight into the potential drivers of DO consumption, we used a conceptual approach to modeling that separately considered chemical and/or biological processes. This was done by testing three different model formulations that represent three assumptions:
a. Chemical processes only (e.g. oxidation of Fe(II), sulfides, and organic matter), assumed to follow first-order (linear) kinetics. In this case, the rate of DO consumption is proportional to the DO concentration in the system, with KL the overall rate constant for chemical reaction (h−1).
b. Biological process only, assumed to follow typical Michaelis-Menten (nonlinear saturating) kinetics.
c. Combined chemical and biological processes, where the consumption of DO was simulated by combining the first two scenarios.
We fit the consumption of DO during incubations using the configurations of Eq 1, 2, and 3 separately. Model parameters were fitted iteratively until the best fit, obtained by least squares adjustment, was achieved. Model fitting was performed with the FME package v1.3.6.1 in R v4.0.3 (Soetaert and Petzoldt, 2010). Model fitness was evaluated by calculating the sum of squares due to regression (SSR).
We explored the relationships among the three different model configurations (chemical, biological, chemical and biological) using kL/Vmax, which represents the relative contribution of chemical (linear) vs. biological (non-linear) processes towards DO consumption.
Detailed description of these equations and models is available in the published paper.

Data analysis
All data analysis was performed using R version 4.2.1 (R Core Team, 2021), with dplyr v1.0.10 for data analysis (Wickham et al., 2021), ggplot2 v3.3.6 and soilpalettes v0.1.0 for data visualization (Wickham, 2016, Patel, 2020), and targets v0.14.0 for reproducible analytical workflows (Landau, 2021).
